claim.title: Colorado reference neuron
claim.lede: This neuron responds most strongly to Colorado-specific context. At generic spaces, punctuation, or function words just before a Colorado place, team, institution, or local phone number, its product rises steeply; the strongest observed anchor was a space before 303-471-74, with product 364. The neuron also promotes tokens such as ' Boulder', ' Colorado', and ' Denver'. Contexts about other interior-Western or northern-Plains places, especially North Dakota and Utah, produce its weaker negative pole.
claim.one_paragraph: The positive pole is sharply localized. Its top anchors sit in passages about Denver, Boulder, Carbondale, Durango, Pikes Peak, Longmont, Aurora, and other Colorado locations, often at a space or punctuation mark before a 303, 720, 719, or 970 telephone number. Across the 30 top positive anchors, gate averaged 18.2 and value 18.3, producing a mean product of 331.4. The distribution is sparse and asymmetric: 32.6% of products are positive, the median is -0.096, and the positive maximum (364.0) is far beyond the negative minimum (-55.25). Token selectivity agrees: above 10% of the maximum product, ' Denver' occurs at 12,438 of 14,277 occurrences (87%), ' Colorado' at 22,011 of 26,215 (84%), and ' Boulder' at 2,902 of 3,905 (74%). The weight-only logit lens raises ' Boulder' by 0.743, ' Colorado' by 0.729, and ' Denver' by 0.722. Ablations alter next-token distributions (median KL 0.112 versus 0.00027 for controls), though positive anchors are stronger and effects vary widely.
claim.negative_pole: The negative pole is weaker and broader. Its strongest anchors fall in text about North Dakota, Utah, New Mexico, Nevada, Arizona, and neighboring interior-Western places, often immediately before or inside non-Colorado telephone numbers such as 435, 701, 505, 603, or 928. The minimum product, -55.25, occurred at a '3' in a Utah 435 number; gate stayed positive (9.94) while value was -5.56, so the negative sign comes from the value channel rather than silence. Across the 30 bottom anchors, gate averaged 7.0 but value averaged -7.2, giving mean product -48.4. Negative tokens are less selective: at 10% of the negative extreme, ' BYU' reaches 15.5% of occurrences and ' Dakota' 14.2%, versus 87% for ' Denver' on the positive side.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: Controlled minimal pairs would be decisive: identical sentences where only Colorado versus another state changes, and the same phone number with different area codes. Strong positive products in clearly North Dakota or Utah passages, or no Colorado-token promotion when place names are varied, would undermine the regional explanation.

claim.title: Colorado local-information neuron
claim.lede: This neuron responds to Colorado local information, not merely to contact formatting. Its strongest products occur at spaces, punctuation, or function words inside Colorado place, team, and local-contact texts; the saved maximum is a space before a 303 number (364.0). It also promotes explicit ' Boulder', ' Colorado', and ' Denver'. A weaker negative pole appears in some off-region public-service, legal, and record contexts, while bare off-region place mentions are inconsistent and often positive.
claim.one_paragraph: The product distribution is sparse and asymmetric: 32.6% of one billion tokens are positive, the median is -0.096, and the positive maximum (364.0) far exceeds the negative minimum (-55.25). The new 434-position semantic sample sharpens the poles. All 19 Colorado local-information and all 7 Colorado sports/culture positions are positive; off-region local records (33), government and legal records (20), health and social services (23), sports commentary (22), and off-region place/culture (37) contain most negative values. These are selected-sample counts, not corpus frequencies, and many constituent contexts are mixed. Token-level selectivity is strong: above 10% of the maximum product, ' Denver' occurs at 12,438 of 14,277 occurrences (87%), ' Colorado' at 22,011 of 26,215 (84%), and ' Boulder' at 2,902 of 3,905 (74%). The weight-only lens promotes ' Boulder' (+0.743), ' Colorado' (+0.729), and ' Denver' (+0.722). At the -55.25 Utah 435 anchor, gate is 9.94 and value -5.56, so the negative sign is value-driven. Zeroing is contextual: across 124 follow-up conditions the median KL is 0.00143 versus 0.00034 for controls, while the 364 maximum gives KL 0.547 and lowers the '3' probability from 0.744 to 0.350.
claim.negative_pole: The negative pole is weaker and not a general anti-Colorado rule. Its natural minimum is -55.25 at a '3' inside a Utah 435 record; across the 30 bottom anchors gate averages 7.0 and value -7.2, giving mean product -48.4. At the fixed record boundary ' as', North Dakota is -17.0 and Fargo -7.125, but Utah is +2.078 and New Mexico -1.039. At the fixed contact boundary ' at', Salt Lake City (+0.945) and Phoenix (+1.133) are mildly positive. The frozen response predictor also called Acoma Pueblo and Fredonia/Dixon negative (they measured +13.625 and +16.375). The reliable negative condition is therefore a specific off-region public-service, legal, or record boundary, not non-Colorado identity alone.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: Strong negative products at explicit Colorado places without any off-region record frame would undermine the regional account. Conversely, uniformly weak or positive products across matched North Dakota and Utah public-service boundaries would reject the negative-pole description; positive responses to generic contact formatting with no regional cue would reject Colorado specificity.

response_rules.name: Colorado area-code phone number
response_rules.description: Product is positive at the token immediately before, or within, a telephone number whose area code is 303, 720, 719, or 970 (for example the space before 303-471-74, product 364.0, or a comma before a 720 number, 332.0), especially after 'call', 'at', 'contact', or 'Phone Number:'.

response_rules.name: Explicit Colorado place, team, or institution
response_rules.description: Product is positive at a token adjacent to or immediately preceding an explicit Colorado name: Denver, Boulder, Colorado, Colorado Springs, Pueblo, Durango, Aspen, Aurora, Longmont, Carbondale, Pikes Peak, 'CO', CU, Broncos, Nuggets, or Rockies. The effect is strongest when the anchor is a generic separator just before the name.

response_rules.name: Generic boundary inside Colorado context
response_rules.description: Product is positive at a space, comma, hyphen, newline, or function word ('at', 'on', 'with', 'to', 'the', 'all', 'above') when the surrounding local window names Colorado places, teams, or Colorado local institutions and the following continuation is a Colorado location, venue, school, or local number.

response_rules.name: Colorado document continuation
response_rules.description: Product is positive when the preceding sentence or heading has established a Colorado locale and the anchor precedes an otherwise ambiguous numeric or capitalised continuation, such as a date, age, school name, or place fragment. This covers anchors that would be uninformative outside the Colorado context.

response_rules.name: Non-Colorado state-local area code
response_rules.description: Product is negative at the token immediately before, or within, a state-local telephone number using a non-Colorado area code such as 435 (Utah), 701 (North Dakota), 505 (New Mexico), 603 (New Hampshire), 928 (Arizona), or 801 (Utah), particularly after 'call', 'contact', 'at', or 'Phone:'. Toll-free 800/888 numbers inherit the surrounding state context.

response_rules.name: North Dakota, Utah, or other interior-West context
response_rules.description: Product is negative at a generic space, comma, or function word in text whose local window centres on North Dakota (Dakota, ND, Fargo, Bismarck, Minot, Badlands), Utah or the Great Basin (BYU, Salt Lake, St. George, Moose, Tahoe), or another non-Colorado interior-Western state or locality.

response_rules.name: No regional cue near anchor
response_rules.description: Product is uncertain in ordinary prose with no nearby Colorado or other interior-Western place, institution, or phone number; the signed product is typically small and its sign is not predictive of a stable concept.

response_rules.name: Conflicting or partial regional cues
response_rules.description: Product is uncertain when Colorado and non-Colorado markers occur in the same local window but neither is adjacent to the anchor, when a toll-free or unlisted area code is the only clue, or when the anchor is an isolated numeric fragment not part of a phone number. Do not infer the pole from the measured sign alone in these boundary cases.

Time Management and Productivity Expert Laura Stack Discusses Strategy and Tactics in the Workplace
In her newest blog, “The MEET Formula Long and the Short of It: Strategy and Tactics in the Modern Workplace,” Stack discusses strategies to achieve certain goals, and the individual steps, or tactics required to achieve those goals.
Since employees are focused on the operational day-to-day activities required to keep revenues flowing, they may not always understand the distinction between the two. It is the responsibility of those in leadership roles to recognize these definitions, and to encourage employees to carve out some time for strategic work or thinking in addition to performing their jobs.
To keep the work team moving forward with an appropriate mix of strategy and tactics, Stack suggests implementing the MEET Formula: Mastermind, Engage, Empower, Tools.
1..Mastermind. Stack suggests a separate meeting to make all staff members aware of big organizational goals, and allow the team time to plan precisely what they need to do to move in the right direction.
“Publish those objectives in a shared space where everyone can access them, and then publically keep track of your group’s progress in future emails and meetings,” Stack says. “Communicate, communicate, and communicate again.”
2. Engage. When team members are excited about their work, Stacks says that those in leadership roles will have an easier time keeping them on track.
“Incentivize them in some way with time off, gift certificates, prizes, trips, or monetary bonuses if certain metrics are achieved,” Stack says. “If they know rewards will come down the line, most will make extra daily efforts to ensure those numbers are hit.”
3. Empower. When team members have the power to make life easier for themselves and for other team members, they’re going to take the initiative to improve group efficiency in ways that pave the way for long term success.
“If there’s no big impact, let them make the changes, additions, and deletions in their time that will achieve the strategic goals,” Stack says. “Stop doing things that no longer add value.”
4. Tools. Make sure staff members have the right tools to accomplish their tasks, so they can build a framework for future success. Providing the right tools and resources improves your team’s engagement and empowerment quotients.
“If you need to pound in a nail and all you have is a wrench, you can do it—but not efficiently,”
“If someone needs a new computer, supply it. If someone requests training, invest in it. If someone wants a smartphone to do work in the evening, get it—even if this person ‘isn’t the right level.’”
Stack reminds her readers of the electronics giant Circuit City that went belly-up by allowing its tactics to overwhelm its strategy, working so hard to make money right away, it forgot to ensure its long-term survival.
Upper management, for example, laid off experienced floor employees en masse, replacing them with cheaper, inexperienced staff. Suddenly, Stack says, the stores were filled with untrained salespeople who didn’t know their own departments, had no idea what they were doing, and had no vision of where the company was going. Long-time employees who survived the purge rapidly disengaged, knowing their jobs remained at risk any time the company wanted to save money.
“Why bother trying anymore?” Stack says.
Circuit City’s profits surged briefly, but customers fled after experiencing the unhelpful sales staff and the general sense that nobody at Circuit City cared. Circuit City landed in Chapter 11 bankruptcy, ruined by its own inept tactics with no connected to a long-term strategy.
Stack reminds readers to maintain a firm grasp on the strategy and the tactics and educate employees on the distinction, and apply the MEET Formula ensure communications are incessant.
“Allowing creative decision making, and provide the tools needed to do their jobs right,” Stack says. “Your employees will keep an eye on the horizon, not just on the task in front of them.”

claim.title: Colorado local-information neuron
claim.lede: This neuron responds to Colorado local information, not merely to contact formatting. Its strongest products occur at spaces, punctuation, or function words inside Colorado place, team, and local-contact texts; the saved maximum is a space before a 303 number (364.0). It also promotes explicit ' Boulder', ' Colorado', and ' Denver'. A weaker negative pole appears in some off-region public-service, legal, and record contexts, while bare off-region place mentions are inconsistent and often positive.
claim.one_paragraph: The product distribution is sparse and asymmetric: 32.6% of one billion tokens are positive, the median is -0.096, and the positive maximum (364.0) far exceeds the negative minimum (-55.25). The new 434-position semantic sample sharpens the poles. All 19 Colorado local-information and all 7 Colorado sports/culture positions are positive; off-region local records (33), government and legal records (20), health and social services (23), sports commentary (22), and off-region place/culture (37) contain most negative values. These are selected-sample counts, not corpus frequencies, and many constituent contexts are mixed. Token-level selectivity is strong: above 10% of the maximum product, ' Denver' occurs at 12,438 of 14,277 occurrences (87%), ' Colorado' at 22,011 of 26,215 (84%), and ' Boulder' at 2,902 of 3,905 (74%). The weight-only lens promotes ' Boulder' (+0.743), ' Colorado' (+0.729), and ' Denver' (+0.722). At the -55.25 Utah 435 anchor, gate is 9.94 and value -5.56, so the negative sign is value-driven. Zeroing is contextual: across 124 follow-up conditions the median KL is 0.00143 versus 0.00034 for controls, while the 364 maximum gives KL 0.547 and lowers the '3' probability from 0.744 to 0.350.
claim.negative_pole: The negative pole is weaker and not a general anti-Colorado rule. Its natural minimum is -55.25 at a '3' inside a Utah 435 record; across the 30 bottom anchors gate averages 7.0 and value -7.2, giving mean product -48.4. At the fixed record boundary ' as', North Dakota is -17.0 and Fargo -7.125, but Utah is +2.078 and New Mexico -1.039. At the fixed contact boundary ' at', Salt Lake City (+0.945) and Phoenix (+1.133) are mildly positive. The frozen response predictor also called Acoma Pueblo and Fredonia/Dixon negative (they measured +13.625 and +16.375). The reliable negative condition is therefore a specific off-region public-service, legal, or record boundary, not non-Colorado identity alone.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: Strong negative products at explicit Colorado places without any off-region record frame would undermine the regional account. Conversely, uniformly weak or positive products across matched North Dakota and Utah public-service boundaries would reject the negative-pole description; positive responses to generic contact formatting with no regional cue would reject Colorado specificity.

response_rules.name: Colorado local phone or contact boundary
response_rules.description: Product is positive at a space, comma, or hyphen immediately before or within a 303, 720, 719, or 970 telephone number, or before a contact value that the local Colorado prefix establishes as a Colorado number, including anchors after 'call', 'at', 'contact', or 'Phone'.

response_rules.name: Explicit Colorado place, team, or institution
response_rules.description: Product is positive at an explicit Colorado place, team, or institution token such as Denver, Boulder, Colorado, Colorado Springs, Pueblo, Durango, Aspen, Aurora, Longmont, Carbondale, Pikes Peak, CO, CU, Broncos, Nuggets, or Rockies, and at an immediately adjacent separator before such a name.

response_rules.name: Boundary inside ongoing Colorado local information
response_rules.description: Product is positive at a generic space, comma, hyphen, newline, or function word when the local prefix has established a Colorado locale and the anchor is a boundary before a local continuation such as an address, phone digit, venue, school, team, or listing value.

response_rules.name: Colorado document continuation
response_rules.description: Product is positive when a sustained Colorado document or heading makes an otherwise ambiguous numeric or capitalized continuation local, for example an MLS or listing number, date, age, school name, or place fragment.

response_rules.name: Off-region public-service or record contact
response_rules.description: Product is negative only when the anchor sits at a separator or digit inside a non-Colorado official public-service, legal, health, or record contact, such as a county sheriff, licensing, statute, or municipal listing, with the off-region state or locality established nearby. Area code alone is insufficient.

response_rules.name: Bare off-region place mention
response_rules.description: Product is uncertain at an off-region place name, generic boundary, or ordinary civic or place-description sentence without a public-service or record-contact frame; these contexts are often near zero and may be positive, as in Acoma Pueblo or a New Mexico press release.

response_rules.name: No regional cue near anchor
response_rules.description: Product is uncertain in ordinary prose with no nearby Colorado or other regional place, institution, or phone cue; such signed products are typically small and do not define a stable concept.

response_rules.name: Conflicting or partial regional cues
response_rules.description: Product is uncertain when Colorado and non-Colorado markers occur in the same local window but neither is adjacent to the anchor, when a toll-free or unlisted area code is the only clue, or when the anchor is an isolated numeric fragment not part of a phone number.

Time Management and Productivity Expert Laura Stack Discusses Strategy and Tactics in the Workplace
In her newest blog, “The MEET Formula Long and the Short of It: Strategy and Tactics in the Modern Workplace,” Stack discusses strategies to achieve certain goals, and the individual steps, or tactics required to achieve those goals.
Since employees are focused on the operational day-to-day activities required to keep revenues flowing, they may not always understand the distinction between the two. It is the responsibility of those in leadership roles to recognize these definitions, and to encourage employees to carve out some time for strategic work or thinking in addition to performing their jobs.
To keep the work team moving forward with an appropriate mix of strategy and tactics, Stack suggests implementing the MEET Formula: Mastermind, Engage, Empower, Tools.
1..Mastermind. Stack suggests a separate meeting to make all staff members aware of big organizational goals, and allow the team time to plan precisely what they need to do to move in the right direction.
“Publish those objectives in a shared space where everyone can access them, and then publically keep track of your group’s progress in future emails and meetings,” Stack says. “Communicate, communicate, and communicate again.”
2. Engage. When team members are excited about their work, Stacks says that those in leadership roles will have an easier time keeping them on track.
“Incentivize them in some way with time off, gift certificates, prizes, trips, or monetary bonuses if certain metrics are achieved,” Stack says. “If they know rewards will come down the line, most will make extra daily efforts to ensure those numbers are hit.”
3. Empower. When team members have the power to make life easier for themselves and for other team members, they’re going to take the initiative to improve group efficiency in ways that pave the way for long term success.
“If there’s no big impact, let them make the changes, additions, and deletions in their time that will achieve the strategic goals,” Stack says. “Stop doing things that no longer add value.”
4. Tools. Make sure staff members have the right tools to accomplish their tasks, so they can build a framework for future success. Providing the right tools and resources improves your team’s engagement and empowerment quotients.
“If you need to pound in a nail and all you have is a wrench, you can do it—but not efficiently,”
“If someone needs a new computer, supply it. If someone requests training, invest in it. If someone wants a smartphone to do work in the evening, get it—even if this person ‘isn’t the right level.’”
Stack reminds her readers of the electronics giant Circuit City that went belly-up by allowing its tactics to overwhelm its strategy, working so hard to make money right away, it forgot to ensure its long-term survival.
Upper management, for example, laid off experienced floor employees en masse, replacing them with cheaper, inexperienced staff. Suddenly, Stack says, the stores were filled with untrained salespeople who didn’t know their own departments, had no idea what they were doing, and had no vision of where the company was going. Long-time employees who survived the purge rapidly disengaged, knowing their jobs remained at risk any time the company wanted to save money.
“Why bother trying anymore?” Stack says.
Circuit City’s profits surged briefly, but customers fled after experiencing the unhelpful sales staff and the general sense that nobody at Circuit City cared. Circuit City landed in Chapter 11 bankruptcy, ruined by its own inept tactics with no connected to a long-term strategy.
Stack reminds readers to maintain a firm grasp on the strategy and the tactics and educate employees on the distinction, and apply the MEET Formula ensure communications are incessant.
“Allowing creative decision making, and provide the tools needed to do their jobs right,” Stack says. “Your employees will keep an eye on the horizon, not just on the task in front of them.”
